text:
The woman who in my blooming

youth could have been

—if God had wished—

mine,


in the inner landscape

of a paradise of love

and poetry;


the one who, noblewoman or peasant,

“my peasant” or “my princess,”

would have been called,

is, in my book, Damiana.


The laughing, holy daughter,

twin of seraphim,

perhaps a dragonfly in my gardens

and an infanta in my realm;


the one who

could give faith to the soul,

vigor to effort, good sense

to action—the one who did not come,

no matter how much I called her!


The one who still kisses my brow

from a distant star,

that one

is, in my book, Damiana.


And the one who looked at me,

I do not know in what beloved homeland,

after looking at me passed on

(this was more than a lifetime ago);


and as she looked at me she seemed

to be saying:

“If I could stop,

I would love you”...


the one who repeated this to me with her eyes;

the one whom, seated at the table

of the royal feast, I awaited

with vain unease, that one

is, in my book, Damiana;


The one who, with noble bearing,

usually wanders fluidly

like a lunar ghost

through the region of my dream;


the one who gleams in sunsets,

which are the day’s nobility,

the one who in the melancholy

of my room feigns footsteps,


the one whom, posted at the window,

with an unceasing longing,

I have awaited for a century,

that one is, in my book, Damiana.


Everything noble and beautiful

that did not come to be;

everything lovely and kind

that did not arrive;


and the vague and mysterious

things I thought,

and the pure and ineffable

and divine;


the enigma always clear in the morning

and the enigma unspoken in the afternoon;

love, dreams, ideal, arcane essence,

all that, all that, all that,

has a name in these pages: Damiana!

translation.title: The Woman Who in My Blooming...
translation.editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s catalog of unrealized women and its recurring identification of them all as Damiana.
